title: Homepage framing: predictable inference + resilient delivery playbook
content:
Objective:

This is a working brief to converge on homepage and above-the-fold messaging that blends two distinct but complementary customer needs: predictable inference economics (unit cost, batching, KV cache) and resilient delivery (graceful fallbacks, routing policies, regional redundancy). The goal is a hero frame that is clearly technical and credible for engineers while remaining approachable for product/platform buyers evaluating cost and SLAs.

Key positioning thesis (one line):
Make inference a predictable, production-grade primitive — consistent latency, accountable unit economics, and automated resilience — so engineering teams ship LLM features without unexpected cost or outages.

Primary audiences and what they care about:
- ML/Platform Engineers: latency SLOs, KV caching, batching, runtime optimizations, rollout control (canary/A-B), easy SDKs.
- Product/PMs: feature velocity, predictable budget, quality guardrails, observable regressions.
- Enterprise buyers/Security: private deployments, VPC, KMS, audit logs, SLAs.

Desired emotional tone and voice: pragmatic, technical, reassuring. Use concrete levers (caching, quantization, routing, fallbacks) rather than vague claims. Avoid hype — show measurable outcomes (latency < X ms, cost per 1k tokens ranges, failure percent with fallback).

Hero copy candidates (10 unique variants) — short and intentionally different:
1) "Ship LLM features that behave in production"
2) "Predictable inference. Fewer surprises."
3) "One API for low-latency, cost-aware LLM serving"
4) "Make inference reliable — routing, fallbacks, and cost controls included"
5) "Latency you can budget for. Quality you can measure."
6) "From prototype to SLA: inference that scales without guesswork"
7) "Control cost, preserve latency, tolerate outages gracefully"
8) "Production-ready LLM serving with predictable economics"
9) "Keep apps online when models fail — automatic fallbacks and routing"
10) "Run LLM inference with the same reliability as your core services"

Subhead and supporting one-liners (pick/iterate):
- "A unified runtime for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — with observability and rollouts built in."
- "Automatically batch, cache, and route requests to meet latency and cost targets."
- "Quantization and model variants recommended per workload; canary and rollback policies included."

Three persona-focused blurbs (short):
- For engineers: "Fine-grained controls: batching, KV cache, kernel selection, and tracing hooks so you debug and optimize token-level cost and latency."
- For platform leads: "Standardize inference across teams with predictable unit economics, quotas, and per-route dashboards."
- For security/compliance: "Private control planes, optional on-prem packages, and audit logs that integrate with your KMS/HSM."

Feature callouts (short bullets for under-hero area):
- High-throughput runtime: continuous batching, optimized kernels, KV cache management
- Smart routing: cost/latency-aware request routing + regional failover
- Rollouts & fallbacks: canary, A/B, automatic fallback to compatible variants
- Cost controls: per-token economics, quantization recommendations, caching suggestions
- Observability: per-route latency/cost breakdowns, token-level traces, eval-linked regressions

Competitive analysis notes (concise, chewable):
- Open model APIs (major public providers): strength = simplicity and scale; weakness = opaque unit economics, limited fallback controls, variable latency under load. Messaging: emphasize Redwood's predictability and policy-driven routing as a counterpoint.
- Cloud managed endpoints (cloud providers): strength = integration with infra; weakness = fragmented UX across regions, limited inference-specific optimizations and rollout tooling. Messaging: Redwood provides inference-first experience and finer controls for model serving.
- Self-hosted runtimes (inference frameworks): strength = control and cost if you invest ops; weakness = ops burden and lack of unified console/rollouts. Messaging: Redwood matches control with less ops surface and turnkey observability + SLAs.

Differentiators to surface on site copy (what to emphasize):
- Predictable unit economics: show examples of cost per 1k tokens with and without caching/batching
- Graceful degradation story: describe how auto-fallback to smaller models or cached responses prevents outages
- Unified deployment modes: same API from hosted to private — highlight migration story
- Operational tooling: per-route dashboards, tracing, rollout controls, and incident playbooks

Hero microcopy CTAs (variants to A/B test):
- Primary CTA: "Get started — free credits" / "Try predictable inference" / "Book a latency deep-dive"
- Secondary CTA: "See cost examples" / "Compare fallbacks" / "Read the routing whitepaper"

Above-the-fold visual & interaction ideas (notes for design):
- Small latency/economics widget under hero that toggles between: median p95 latency, estimated $/1M tokens, and fallback rate.
- Quick 3-step schematic: 1) Route requests by policy 2) Cache & batch 3) Observe & roll out — with microcopy explaining SLOs.

SEO and keyword targets to weave into page copy and meta: "LLM inference platform", "predictable inference costs", "production LLM serving", "model rollouts", "inference routing", "inference fallback", "dedicated GPU serving"

Copy testing plan (12-week):
- Week 0–2: Internal alignment and microcopy A/B candidates instrumented for GA experiments (primary CTA + top 3 hero headlines).
- Week 3–6: Run holdouts by new signups and click-through; track metrics: CTR hero -> signup, time-to-token-first-API-call, demo requests.
- Week 7–12: Qual interviews with 8 trial customers (engineer + PM), refine technical claims with quantifiable numbers from infra team (p95 latency targets, cost-savings examples).

Key metrics to validate copy efficacy:
- Hero CTA CTR (target > 6% for initial experiment)
- Signups from organic homepage traffic (target +15% vs baseline)
- Demo/latency-deep-dive conversion rate (qualitative signal for enterprise interest)

Microcopy examples for nearby product pages (short):
- "Dedicated: reserved GPU pools, SLA-backed latency"
- "Private: VPC, KMS, audit-ready deployments"
- "Optimize: batching and quantization suggestions tailored to your prompts"

Risks and open questions (explicit):
- We may over-index on "predictability" language that sounds like financial guarantees; need to ensure legal & infra can support claims (ask legal + infra for safe language).
- Do we show explicit numbers (ms, $) or ranges? If yes, which workloads to base on? (follow up with benchmarks team).
- Funnel risk: too technical hero may deter product buyers — plan to use layered copy (technical toggles, link to deeper docs).

Next steps and owners:
- Get infra/benchmarks (Lars) to supply p50/p95 numbers and a representative cost table for small/medium/large sequences — due 2025-03-04.
- Draft 3 final hero variants and design comps (Nikhil + design) — due 2025-03-07.
- Legal review on public cost/latency statements (Maya) — due 2025-03-10.
- Instrument A/B experiment in launch page (growth) with tracking plan — due 2025-03-14.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is deliberately heavy on concrete mechanics (routing, caching, fallbacks). If you think the hero should be more emotive, propose a variant and mark it in comments.
- Please flag any competitor claims that feel dismissive; keep neutral comparisons.

Appendix: example short narrative to test as long-form lead paragraph (for product page or expanded hero drawer):

"Most LLM problems in production aren't model quality — they're predictability and reliability. Requests that spike tokens, unexpected model downtimes, and fragmented deployment modes all create cost and outage risk. Redwood removes the guesswork: a unified runtime that batches and caches, routes requests according to policy, and falls back automatically to compatible variants. The result: predictable token economics, consistent latency, and an inference layer you can operate like any other core service."

End of brief.
